title: The measure of bliss: from the happiest of men to Brahman
theme: Everything works from awe of Brahman; then an inquiry measures bliss in steps of a hundred, from the happiest human life to Brahman, says at each step that the learned one free of desire already has it, and ends with the knower passing through the five selves.

sandhi.type: vowel sandhi; final t before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: bhīṣā + asmāt: ā + a → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः). asmāt before the voiced v becomes asmād, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
The visarga before c becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः), and s becomes ś before c, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः). ca + indraḥ: a + i → e, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).
The visarga of mṛtyuḥ goes back to s, which becomes ru, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः); before the voiced dh it is written r.
sā + eṣā: ā + e → ai, P. 6.1.88 (वृद्धिरेचि). eṣā + ānandasya: ā + ā → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes o: the visarga (ru) becomes u, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u → o.

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: The visarga becomes y before a vowel, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the two vowels then stay apart.

samasa.meaning: a young man who is good. Śaṅkara explains why both are said: a young man may be bad, and a good man may not be young.

morphology.note: A Vedic instrumental of the root noun bhī, ‘fear’ (classical bhiyā): ‘through fear’. The same three lines, with bhayāt, are Kaṭha 2.3.3.
Optative of as, ‘to be’, used for a supposition: ‘let there be a young man …’ — the imagined case from which the measure of bliss starts.

Superlative in -iṣṭha. Classical grammar replaces the ṛ of dṛḍha by ra before this suffix (draḍhiṣṭha), P. 6.4.161 (र ऋतो हलादेर्लघोः); the ‘आ.भा.’ passage and Gopālānanda write so («द्रढिष्ठः अतिशयेन दृढः»). The Upaniṣad keeps ṛ.

A superlative in -iṣṭha whose base is not certain. Śaṅkara takes it from ā-śās, ‘to direct’ («आशास्तृतमः»), the ‘आ.भा.’ passage from āśu, ‘quick’ («अनलसतया क्षिप्रकारी»), Gopālānanda from aś, ‘to eat’ («अशनसमर्थः»).

translation.literal: Out of fear of this [Brahman] the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises; out of fear of this, Agni and Indra, [and] Death runs, the fifth. This is the inquiry into bliss. Let there be a young man, a good young man, learned [in the Veda], most able, firmest, strongest; let this whole earth, full of wealth, be his. That is one human bliss. Those which are a hundred human blisses —
translation.readable: Through fear of it the wind blows; through fear of it the sun rises; through fear of it fire and Indra, and Death as the fifth, keep to their work. Now an inquiry into bliss. Imagine a young man, good, well-learned, quick, firm and strong, who owns the whole earth and all its wealth: his joy is one unit of human bliss. A hundred of these —

morphology.note: Genitive plural of pitṛ with long ṝ before -ṇām. The Sāyaṇa-pāṭha keys पितृणां with short ṛ (corrections.json: spelling only).
The genitive stands without a verb: ‘[this bliss is] of the śrotriya, too’. The line follows each step from here to the end, but not the first (human) step; see the commentary.

translation.literal: — that is one bliss of the human gandharvas, and of the śrotriya not struck by desire. Those which are a hundred blisses of the human gandharvas, that is one bliss of the divine gandharvas, and of the śrotriya not struck by desire. Those which are a hundred blisses of the divine gandharvas, that is one bliss of the ancestors whose world lasts long, and of the śrotriya not struck by desire. Those which are a hundred blisses of the ancestors whose world lasts long, that is one bliss of the gods born in the ājāna —
translation.readable: — make one bliss of the gandharvas who were once men; and that bliss belongs also to one learned in the Veda whom desire does not strike down. A hundred of those make one bliss of the gandharvas born divine — and it is his too. A hundred of those make one bliss of the ancestors in their long-lasting world — and it is his too. A hundred of those make one bliss of the gods born in the gods’ world —

translation.literal: — and of the śrotriya not struck by desire. Those which are a hundred blisses of Indra, that is one bliss of Bṛhaspati, and of the śrotriya not struck by desire. sandhi.type: saḥ before a consonant; visarga before c; vowel sandhi
sandhi.rule: saḥ drops its ending before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि). yaḥ ca → yaś ca, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः) with P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः). ca + ayam → cāyam, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
asau + āditye: au before a vowel becomes āv, P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः).
A final t before l becomes l, P. 8.4.60 (तोर्लि): asmāl lokāt.
A final m before a vowel is written together with it.

tat before a vowel → tad, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते); api + eṣaḥ → apy eṣaḥ, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि); eṣaḥ drops its ending before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि); ślokaḥ before bh → śloko, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).

samasa.meaning: one who knows thus; vid is a root noun (suffix kvip, P. 3.2.76 (क्विप् च))

morphology.note: The suffix -maya (mayaṭ) can mean ‘made of’ or ‘abounding in’; P. 5.4.21 (तत्प्रकृतवचने मयट्) gives the second sense. Gopālānanda takes ānandamaya as ‘abundance of bliss’ («आनन्दमयशब्दाभिप्रेतम् आनन्दप्राचुर्यं»); whether the ānandamaya is Brahman itself is argued in the Brahmasūtra (BS 1.1.12).
Present of kram, ‘to step’, with upa and sam: ‘steps up to, passes into’. Whether the step is literal is the main question of the unit (see commentary).
Absolutive of i with pra, ‘having gone forth’; in many texts ‘having died’. Śaṅkara takes it here as turning away from the world of objects.

translation.literal: He who is this one in the person, and he who is that one in the sun — he is one. He who knows thus, having gone forth from this world, passes into this self made of food, passes into this self made of breath, passes into this self made of mind, passes into this self made of understanding, passes into this self made of bliss. On that too there is this verse:
translation.readable: The one who is here in the person and the one who is there in the sun are one. Whoever knows this, on leaving this world, passes into the self made of food, then the self made of breath, the self made of mind, the self made of understanding, and the self made of bliss. On this there is a verse:

syntax: Four short clauses of cause (bhīṣā … pavate, udeti; Agni, Indra and Death sharing dhāvati) introduce a nominal announcement (‘sā eṣā ānandasya mīmāṃsā bhavati’). The measure begins with optatives of supposition (yuvā syāt …, pṛthivī … tasya syāt) and a nominal sentence (sa eko mānuṣa ānandaḥ). Then one sentence-pattern is repeated ten times: a relative clause ‘te ye śataṃ X-ānām ānandāḥ’ (those which are a hundred blisses of X) taken up by ‘sa ekaḥ Y-ānām ānandaḥ’ (that is one bliss of Y), followed by the verbless genitive ‘śrotriyasya cākāmahatasya’ (and [it is] the śrotriya’s). One step has an explanatory relative clause (ye karmaṇā devān apiyanti). 2.8.5 is a relative–correlative identity (sa yaś cāyaṃ … yaś cāsāv … sa ekaḥ), then five parallel main clauses with the same verb, and a formula introducing a verse.

ambiguities.topic: Whose bliss is at the top: Brahmā’s or Brahman’s?
ambiguities.note: brahmaṇaḥ is the genitive of both masculine brahman (Brahmā) and neuter brahman. Śaṅkara takes it as Hiraṇyagarbha, the cosmic Brahmā («स एष हिरण्यगर्भो ब्रह्मा»), whose bliss is still a fragment of the supreme. Kūranārāyaṇa takes it as the lotus-born lord of one cosmic egg («स्वनाभिपद्मजन्य-एकाण्डाधिपतेः»), as does Madhva («तस्माद् ब्रह्मा शतगुणो मुक्त इत्येष निर्णयः»). Gopālānanda takes it as the supreme Brahman named at the beginning of the vallī («ब्रह्मविदाप्नोति परम् इति प्रस्तुतस्य परस्य ब्रह्मणः आनन्दः»), and adds that ‘one’ does not limit it («न च एक इति निर्देशात् ब्रह्मानन्दस्य परिच्छिन्नता»); the ‘आ.भा.’ passage says the same («प्रजापतेः आनन्दतः शतगुणोत्कर्षवान् आनन्दः प्रकृतस्य आनन्दमयस्य इत्यर्थः»).

Śaṅkara: Virāj, the cosmic person whose body is the three worlds («प्रजापतिः विराट् त्रैलोक्यशरीरो»). The ‘आ.भा.’ passage: the four-faced Brahmā («प्रजापतिश्च अत्र चतुर्मुखो ब्रह्मा»). Madhva (cited verses): Rudra, lord of procreation («तस्मात् प्रजापतिर्मुक्तो रुद्रः प्रजननेशिता»).

Śaṅkara: one who has studied the Veda («अध्यायकः अधीतवेदः»). Gopālānanda and the ‘आ.भा.’ passage gloss it as a teacher of his own age-group («यूनां समवयसाम् अध्यापकः»). The text’s word is adhyāyaka; the second reading treats it as adhyāpaka.

The base of this superlative is uncertain (morphology). Śaṅkara: most able to command («आशास्तृतमः»); the ‘आ.भा.’ passage: quickest, not lazy («अनलसतया क्षिप्रकारी»); Gopālānanda: best able to eat, i.e. healthy («अशनसमर्थः»); Kūranārāyaṇa gives several, ‘of wide fame’ among them («आशिष्ठः पृथुकीर्तिः»).

pretya often means ‘having died’. Śaṅkara takes it as withdrawing from the world of objects while living («अस्माल्लोकात्प्रेत्य प्रत्यावृत्य निरपेक्षो भूत्वा»). Gopālānanda, Kūranārāyaṇa and the ‘आ.भा.’ passage take it as departure after death by the path of light («अर्चिरादिना मार्गेण निर्गतः»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose. The opening lines on fear recall a verse (Kaṭha 2.3.3 has them as an anuṣṭubh with bhayāt), but here they are not metrical.

beginner: This passage tries to measure happiness. It starts with the happiest person you can imagine: young, good, educated, quick, strong, healthy, and owner of the whole world and all its riches. His joy counts as one unit. A hundred of those units make the joy of a heavenly singer; a hundred of those make the joy of another, higher kind of being; and so on, ten times, each step a hundred times greater, up to the joy of Brahman. At every step after the first the text adds a surprising line: a learned person who is not driven by wanting things already has that joy. The point is not the numbers. It is that joy grows as wanting falls away. Then the text says the one in us and the one in the sun are the same, and that whoever knows this passes, layer by layer, into the self made of bliss.
analogy: Like an old surveyor who measures a mountain by stacking a familiar staff again and again: the staff is ordinary, the count becomes absurd, and the point is that the mountain is beyond any staff.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Out of fear of ‘this’ the wind blows, the sun rises, Agni, Indra and Death do their work. Then ‘the inquiry into bliss’: the bliss of a young, good, learned, able, firm, strong man who owns the whole wealthy earth is one human bliss; a hundred of those are one bliss of the human gandharvas; and so on, each a hundredfold — divine gandharvas, ancestors, gods born in the ājāna, gods by rite, gods, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, Brahman. From the second step on, each bliss is said to be also ‘the śrotriya’s, not struck by desire’. Then: the one in the person and the one in the sun are one; the one who knows thus, going forth from this world, passes into the selves made of food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss. A verse follows (2.9).

commentary.q: Why do the powers of nature act ‘out of fear’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads the lines as proof that there is a ruler: great and free beings keep to toilsome tasks only because someone governs them («तस्मादस्ति भयकारणं तेषां प्रशास्तृ ब्रह्म»), like servants under a king («यतस्ते भृत्या इव राज्ञः अस्मात् ब्रह्मणः भयेन प्रवर्तन्ते»). Kūranārāyaṇa cites the Brahmasūtra («कम्पनात्») and the Kaṭha verse, and draws a lesson for worship: even the gods one might worship live in fear, so no lasting joy is to be had from them. Gopālānanda: not only the breathing of creatures but every working of the elements, the planets and death depends on the Self of bliss («सर्वम् आनन्दमयायत्तम्»). In the digital text of Madhva these lines are commented on at the end of his section on 2.7: the gods, though knowers, do their work in fear, to please Viṣṇu («भीताः स्वकर्म कुर्वन्ति विष्णोः प्रीत्यर्थमञ्जसा»).

commentary.q: What is the ‘inquiry into bliss’ inquiring?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: whether the bliss of Brahman is like worldly joy, produced by contact of subject and object, or natural to it («किमानन्दो विषयविषयिसम्बन्धजनितः लौकिकानन्दवत् , आहोस्वित् स्वाभाविकः, इत्येवमेषा आनन्दस्य मीमांसा»). Worldly joy is itself a fragment of Brahman’s bliss («लौकिकोऽप्यानन्दः ब्रह्मानन्दस्यैव मात्रा»), as another Upaniṣad says («एतस्यैवानन्दस्यान्यानि भूतानि मात्रामुपजीवन्ति»), and the scale is a way to lead the mind from the known joy to the unknown. The ‘आ.भा.’ passage puts it as a measuring rod: the emperor’s joy is fixed as the unit by which the others are measured («अयमेव आनन्दो मानदण्डस्थानीयः स्थिरीकृतः»).

commentary.q: Why is the learned one ‘not struck by desire’ named at every step but the first?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara finds three means named in the passage — learning in the Veda, freedom from fault, and freedom from desire — and only the third varies («तस्मादेतानि त्रीणि साधनानीत्यवगम्यते»): as desire for each lower level falls away, the bliss of the higher level is directly known, so freedom from desire is taught as the means to the highest bliss («अकामहतत्वस्य परमानन्दप्राप्तिसाधनत्वविधानार्थम्»). The phrase first appears at the second step to say that one not struck by desire for human pleasures has a joy equal to a human gandharva’s («प्रथमं तु अकामहताग्रहणं मनुष्यविषयभोगकामानभिहतस्य श्रोत्रियस्य मनुष्यानन्दात् शतगुणेन आनन्दोत्कर्षः मनुष्यगन्धर्वेण तुल्यो वक्तव्य इत्येवमर्थम्»). The ‘आ.भा.’ passage gives another reason: the learned one does not seek the human joy at all, being without passion for it («अयं च आनन्दः श्रोत्रियेण विदुषा न अनुभूयते»).

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: For Śaṅkara the scale ends with Hiraṇyagarbha, in whom these degrees of bliss become one; his bliss is still a measured fragment of the supreme bliss, of which the others are drops of spray from the ocean («यस्य मात्रा समुद्राम्भस इव विप्रुषः प्रविभक्ताः»); the supreme bliss is natural and non-dual («स एष परमानन्दः स्वाभाविकः, अद्वैतात्»). Madhva’s verses read the whole scale as a scale of the released: even in liberation bliss differs («स्यादेव मोक्षस्तत्रापि ह्यानन्दस्य विचित्रता»), each step a hundredfold, up to Brahmā. Gopālānanda and the ‘आ.भा.’ passage make the last step the supreme Brahman, and explain that the number only says it surpasses Prajāpati’s bliss, as ‘the sun moves like an arrow’ says only that it is not slow («इषुवत् सविता गच्छति»).

commentary.q: What does ‘the one in the person and the one in the sun are one’ mean?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the supreme Self, entered into the body and also the bliss shown in the sun, is one, as space in different pots is one space («भिन्नप्रदेशघटाकाशाकाशैकत्ववत्»); the sun is named to show that no height or lowness remains for the knower. Kūranārāyaṇa identifies the person in the sun with the golden person of the Chāndogya, the lotus-eyed Lord («पुरुषः पुण्डरीकाक्षः पीताम्बररूपी उपास्यत्वेन उच्यते»). Gopālānanda: the one in the heart and the one in the sun are one deity, to be meditated on in the heart with that divine form («हृदयगुहावर्तितया तादृशदिव्यविग्रहविशिष्टत्वेन च ध्यानं कर्तव्यम्»).

commentary.q: Does the knower really ‘pass into’ the five selves?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara argues at length that no movement is meant: the all-pervading Self cannot travel, and a self cannot step into itself; ‘passing into’ is a figure for knowledge that destroys the mistaken identification with the sheaths («विज्ञानमात्रं सङ्क्रमणश्रुतेरर्थः», «न जलूकादिवत् सङ्क्रमणमिहोपदिश्यते»). Gopālānanda: the knower departs after death by the path of light and reaches the Self of bliss, so the text marks a difference between the one who attains and what is attained, and a journey to a place («प्राप्तृप्राप्ययोः भेदः देशविशेषगमनं चेति मुक्तौ विशेषः निरूपितः भवति»). Kūranārāyaṇa likewise refers it to the path of light («अर्चिरादिमार्गः»).

commentary.q: Why the superlatives, and what kind of word is ‘bhīṣā’?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: bhīṣā is an old instrumental of bhī, ‘fear’, kept in the Veda; the same three lines appear in the Kaṭha with bhayāt. The young man is described by three superlatives in -iṣṭha (āśiṣṭha, dṛḍhiṣṭha, baliṣṭha); the first has no agreed base, and the commentators give four different senses (ambiguities). The repeated pattern ‘te ye śataṃ … sa ekaḥ …’ is a relative–correlative pair: ‘those hundred … that is one …’.

advaita.text: The graded joys are fragments of one bliss, appearing as many because of ignorance; when the division into subject and object made by ignorance is removed, one natural, complete, non-dual bliss remains («निरस्ते त्वविद्याकृते विषयविषयिविभागे, विद्यया स्वाभाविकः परिपूर्णः एकः आनन्दः अद्वैतः»). The knower does not travel: ‘passing into’ the selves is knowledge removing the error of taking the sheaths for the Self.

visistadvaita.text: The person in the heart and in the sun is the Lord with a divine form, to be meditated on. The released departs by the path of light and attains him, remaining distinct from him: Gopālānanda reads the verb as marking a difference between attainer and attained. Kūranārāyaṇa discusses whether the released experiences Brahman as other or as his own self, and answers that, being Brahman’s body and mode, he enjoys Brahman’s qualities with Brahman as his own Self («ब्रह्मशरीरतया ब्रह्मप्रकारभूतत्वात् स्वात्मभूतेन ब्रह्मणा सह तद्गुणान् अनुभवतीति वदति»).

dvaita.ref: Taittirīyopaniṣad-bhāṣya on the ānanda-mīmāṃsā (abridged in the digital text)
dvaita.text: The steps of the scale are steps among the released: liberation is certain for the knowers, yet bliss in it differs («स्यादेव मोक्षस्तत्रापि ह्यानन्दस्य विचित्रता»), each class a hundredfold above the one before, up to Brahmā; the same holds for knowledge, devotion to Viṣṇu and strength. Madhva’s comment is reported from the verses he cites; the digital text marks it as abridged.

schools.disagreement: All three read the scale as leading the mind beyond every measured joy. They differ on what lies at the end and what the knower gains. For Śaṅkara the degrees belong to ignorance and dissolve into one bliss that the knower is. For the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators the released reaches the Lord, distinct from him, and enjoys his bliss as his body. For Madhva the degrees continue in liberation itself.

parallels.note: The same five powers acting in fear of Brahman, in verse; cited here by Kūranārāyaṇa.

parallels.quote: स यो मनुष्याणां राद्धः समृद्धो भवत्यन्येषामधिपतिः
parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s own scale of bliss, also in steps of a hundred and also with ‘yaś ca śrotriyo ’vṛjino ’kāmahataḥ’, with a different order of beings.
The Brahmasūtra section on whether the self made of bliss is Brahman, argued from the repetition of ‘bliss’ in this vallī; the schools read the sūtra differently.

contemporary.text: The scale begins where most ambition ends: youth, health, education, ability and the whole world’s wealth. The Upaniṣad treats that as the smallest unit and then says, at every step, that someone free of desire already has more. Those who study happiness often say that more income adds less and less once needs are met, and that wanting more can spoil what one has. The passage makes a sharper claim: the measure of joy is not what one owns but how little one is driven. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you imagine the happiest possible life, what is in it? Which of those things depend on wanting?
reflect.deeper: The text says the learned one free of desire already has each higher joy. Is freedom from desire a means to joy, or is it the joy itself?
reflect.practice: Notice one moment today when you are content without having got anything. Stay with it for a few breaths before moving on.

references.text: Śaṅkara’s comment on 2.8.5 contains a long debate on how the knower can ‘pass into’ the self of bliss if he is not other than it; it is summarised above.

Madhva’s bhāṣya on this anuvāka is marked as abridged in the digital text (it begins with ‘…..’), and his comment on the opening lines about fear stands at the end of his section on 2.7; his views are reported from the verses that survive.

The ‘आ.भा.’ passages (attribution uncertain; most likely Rāmānanda’s Ānandabhāṣya) here name the goal as the abode called Sāketa and the Lord as Śrī Rāma («साकेताख्यं देशविशेषं», «श्रीरामपदप्रसिद्धम्»), which fits a Rāmānandī author. Raṅgarāmānuja and Govindarāja have no comment on this anuvāka in the imported text.

flags.note: The base file keys the last ‘cākāmahatasya’ as चाकामहातस्य; corrected (corrections.json). The space inside mīmāṃsā in the base file is also corrected. The Sāyaṇa-pāṭha writes pitṛṇām with short ṛ (spelling).
Madhva’s text as keyed lacks sarvā (‘the whole earth’) and one devānām; both are marked for verification against a printed Madhva bhāṣya (corrections.json).
Whether the top of the scale (brahmaṇaḥ) is Brahmā or the supreme Brahman, and who Prajāpati is, are decided differently by the commentators (ambiguities).
The derivation of āśiṣṭha is uncertain; four senses are given by the commentators.
